note: Every factual statement the app makes outside a recipe lives here, attached to the sources in citations.json. If a claim cannot be sourced, it does not belong in this file — and it does not belong on the screen.

topics.title: Food is nourishment first
topics.lede: Most eating advice starts from restriction — what to cut, avoid, and feel guilty about. That framing is exhausting and it does not last. This app starts somewhere else: food is how you take care of the people at your table, and the meal that gets cooked again next month is worth more than the perfect meal that gets cooked once.
body: Nothing here asks you to eat less. It asks a different question — what could go *on* the plate that makes it better. More plants, more fiber, more color, more flavor built from technique instead of salt. The things that get crowded out get crowded out quietly.
There is no streak to break, no points, no red numbers. A week where you cook twice is a good week. The tool is here to make the cooking easier, not to keep score.

claims.text: Most people eat around half the fiber associated with the lowest risk of early death — the sweet spot in the evidence sits between 25 g and 30 g a day.
Eating more fiber-rich food is linked to lower blood pressure and lower cholesterol in trials, not only to lower risk in population studies.
People who eat more than 30 different plant foods in a week carry a more diverse set of gut bacteria than people who eat 10 or fewer.
claims.detail: Thirty is a useful nudge toward variety rather than a threshold with a health outcome attached. Herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, grains and pulses all count toward it.

topics.title: What happens at the table
topics.lede: Cooking gets all the attention, and then the meal is eaten in eleven minutes standing near the counter. The twenty minutes after the pan comes off the heat are cheap to improve and almost nobody thinks about them — so here is what is actually known, and what is only a good habit.
body: Three of the four things on this list cost nothing and take no equipment: the order you eat a plate in, how fast you eat it, and whether you stand up afterward. None of them are treatments for anything. They are small, free, and better supported than most of what gets said about eating.
The fourth is water, where the confident advice in circulation is mostly invented. The honest version is shorter than the folklore.

claims.text: Eating the vegetables and protein of a meal before its carbohydrate lowered the blood-glucose rise afterward by roughly a third at 30 and 60 minutes, compared with the same meal eaten carbohydrate-first.
claims.detail: Eleven adults with type 2 diabetes, the same 628-calorie meal twice a week apart. It measures the shape of the curve after single meals rather than any long-term outcome, and the effect depends on the parts of the plate actually being eaten separately — a stew mixes them for you. Free to try, and not a reason to change anything a clinician has told you.

claims.text: Across many experiments, people served the same meal ate less of it when they ate more slowly, and reported no more hunger afterward.
claims.detail: Fullness signals take time to arrive and fast eating outruns them. These are single-meal laboratory studies of how much gets eaten, not trials of long-term eating or health. Putting the fork down between bites is the entire intervention.

claims.text: Short bouts of light walking that break up sitting lowered post-meal glucose and insulin significantly compared with staying seated — including bouts of only a few minutes.
claims.detail: Pooled from acute studies measuring the hours after a meal in small samples. Clearing the table and washing up counts. It is one of the cheapest habits available and that is the whole claim being made for it.

claims.text: For people with reflux, gastroenterology guidance recommends leaving two to three hours between the last meal and lying down.
claims.detail: This is guidance for people who have symptoms, not a rule about when everybody should eat dinner. There is no clock at which food becomes fat.

claims.text: The adequate intake for total water is about 3.7 liters a day for men and 2.7 for women, counting every drink and the water in food — roughly a fifth of it arrives in food.
claims.detail: An adequate intake is the median of what apparently well-hydrated people consume, not a target to hit, and there is no eight-glass rule in any guideline. Coffee and tea count. Heat, exercise, illness and medication all move it, and heart or kidney conditions can come with fluid limits from a clinician that override anything an app says.

claims.text: Drinking water with a meal does not dilute stomach acid enough to matter, and there is no evidence it impairs digestion.
claims.detail: Included because the opposite is repeated confidently and often. The stomach regulates its own acid secretion, and a glass of water has left it long before digestion is finished.

claims.text: A full ENERGY STAR certified dishwasher uses about 3.2 gallons of water a cycle, against up to 27 gallons for washing the same load by hand under a running tap.
claims.detail: Three conditions carry it: run it full, skip the pre-rinse, and use the normal cycle. The 27-gallon figure assumes the tap runs the whole time — washing in a filled basin closes most of the gap, and that is the honest comparison for anybody without a machine.

topics.title: What food does to a heart — and what it doesn't
topics.lede: If someone in your family has heart disease, you have probably been handed a list of things to stop. Here is the more useful version: what the evidence actually shows food can do, how it works, and — just as importantly — where its power ends.

sections.title: How diet actually reaches the heart
body: Arteries narrow over decades as cholesterol-carrying particles lodge in the artery wall and inflame it. Blood pressure decides how hard the heart has to push against those vessels every minute of every day. Diet acts on both — mostly through which fats you eat, how much sodium and potassium you get, and how much fiber passes through you.
None of this is fast, and none of it is visible. It is a slow change in the conditions inside your blood vessels, which is exactly why it is easy to disbelieve and easy to abandon.

claims.text: Replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated vegetable oil lowered cardiovascular disease by about 30% in randomized trials — an effect the American Heart Association notes is similar in size to statin treatment.
claims.detail: The benefit is in the swap. Cutting saturated fat and replacing it with refined starch or sugar does not produce the same result, which is why this app cooks with olive oil rather than simply cooking with less.

claims.text: A Mediterranean-style pattern with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts cut heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular death by roughly 30% over five years in a randomized trial of nearly 7,500 people at high risk.
claims.detail: This trial was retracted and republished in 2018 after randomization problems at some sites. The reanalysis reached the same conclusions. We cite the corrected version, and we mention the retraction because a citation engine that hides inconvenient history is decoration.

claims.text: Swapping ordinary salt for a potassium-based salt substitute reduced stroke by about 14% and death by about 12% in a five-year randomized trial of nearly 21,000 people.
claims.detail: Potassium-based substitutes are not safe for everyone — kidney disease and some blood-pressure medications make them risky. Ask a clinician before switching. The broader point stands on its own: sodium is worth taking seriously, and most of it arrives from packaged food and restaurant food rather than the salt shaker.

claims.text: People eating the most dietary fiber had 15–30% lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality than those eating the least.
Oats and barley carry an FDA-authorised heart-disease health claim at 3 g of beta-glucan soluble fiber a day.

sections.title: Where food's power ends
body: This is the part most food apps leave out, and leaving it out does real harm — it sets people up to feel that a heart attack was a personal failure of willpower.

Diet is one input among several. Genetics, age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, sleep, stress and access to care all matter, and some of them matter more than what is for dinner. Roughly 1 in 250 people inherits a condition that keeps LDL cholesterol high no matter how carefully they eat.

Food does not clear an existing blockage, does not replace a prescription, and does not make anyone immortal. What it reliably does is shift the odds and improve how you feel while doing it. That is worth a great deal, and it is not the same as control.

claims.text: In inherited high cholesterol, lifestyle change is an adjunct to medication and is unlikely to reach treatment targets on its own.
Major cholesterol guidelines treat a heart-healthy dietary pattern as the foundation for everyone, and drug therapy as necessary on top of it for defined risk groups — not as an either/or.
Nothing in this app is medical advice, and no score here is a diagnosis. If someone you cook for has heart disease, their clinician sets the targets; this app just helps you hit them at dinner.

topics.title: What it means for the planet
topics.lede: Food is one of the largest levers an ordinary household actually controls. Not the only one, and not a substitute for the decisions made by governments and energy companies — but a real one, exercised three times a day.

claims.text: Food systems account for roughly a quarter to a third of global greenhouse gas emissions — 26% by one widely cited estimate, 34% by another using a broader boundary.
claims.detail: The two estimates differ because they draw the system boundary differently, not because one is wrong. The IPCC's own range is 21–37%. We quote the range rather than the most dramatic number in it.

claims.text: Animal products use around 83% of the world's farmland while providing about 18% of its calories and 37% of its protein.
A global shift away from animal products would cut farmland use by around 76% and food's greenhouse gas emissions by roughly half.
claims.detail: That is a global thought experiment, not a prediction and not a demand. The practical read is directional: moving some meals toward plants moves the number, and the size of the shift scales with how much you actually change.

claims.text: Impact varies enormously between producers of the same food — so where something was grown can matter as much as what it is.
claims.detail: This cuts against tidy rules. It is also why this app does not put a carbon score on every recipe: the honest error bars would be wider than the differences we would be claiming to show.

topics.title: What it means for the grocery bill
topics.lede: The idea that eating well is expensive is half true — it depends entirely on what you buy. Dried lentils, oats, cabbage, frozen vegetables and canned beans are among the cheapest calories in any store, and they are also among the most nutritious.

claims.text: Modeled across 150 countries, vegetarian and vegan patterns cost 21–34% less than the current typical diet in high-income countries; a low-meat flexitarian pattern about 14% less.
claims.detail: This models retail food prices only. It does not count your time, your kitchen, or whether the cheap options are stocked where you shop — all of which are real costs, and none of which show up in a price index.

claims.text: The savings come from the substitutions, not from buying speciality products. Meat substitutes and packaged plant foods are frequently more expensive than the meat they replace.
claims.detail: Which is why almost nothing in this collection calls for a meat substitute. Beans, lentils, eggs, tofu, grains and whatever is in season do the work.

topics.title: What it means for animals
topics.lede: This app does not tell you what to believe about eating animals. It does think you are entitled to the number, stated plainly and without a photograph attached.

claims.text: More than 80 billion land animals were slaughtered for meat worldwide in 2022, the great majority of them chickens.
claims.detail: That count excludes fish and other aquatic animals, which are reported by weight rather than by individual, and excludes animals that die in egg and dairy production.

claims.text: Every dinner here is built to be complete without meat, with meat available as an addition. That is a design choice about flexibility, not a verdict on anyone's eating.
claims.detail: One table often holds a vegetarian, an omnivore, a teenager who has just announced something, and someone under doctor's orders. Cooking one base everybody can eat is simply the practical answer to that, and it happens to move all three of the numbers above.
